The tryouts for the college softball team were in two hours, and she still hadn't packed her bat bag or eaten breakfast. She had been training for months, pouring every ounce of energy into perfecting her swing and developing a wicked throw from third base. Tonight was her chance to finally make it onto the team.

As she walked over to the TV, flipping through channels out of habit rather than interest, Jena's mind started racing with worst-case scenarios. What if she didn't make the cut? Would she have to transfer schools, lose a whole year of eligibility? The thought made her stomach twist in knots as she absent-mindedly picked at a hangnail on her left hand.

By the time tryouts rolled around, Jena's hands were shaking and her legs felt like lead. She took several deep breaths as she sat waiting on the bench, running through mental checklists of all the things that had gone right – or wrong – over the past few months.

As their names started being called one by one to take swings in front of Coach Anderson, Jena's anxiety only grew. What if someone else took her spot? Would she ever get the chance to compete at this level?

When it was finally her turn on deck, she felt like she was wading through quicksand – every step forward felt weighed down by doubts and fears.

Marcus rubbed his sweaty palms together as he stood in line for a slice of pizza with his team. Their tryout for the school football squad had wrapped up hours ago, but they still lingered around, reluctant to give up what little bit of adrenaline remained coursing through their veins.

For what felt like an eternity – though it was probably only minutes – Coach Thompson stood on that field, giving some guy from a rival school a once-over before deciding against making him part of the team. As Marcus watched the other boy walk away dejected, he could almost feel his own heart sink – not with disappointment, exactly, but with something just shy of dread.

Marcus took another deep breath as the pizza shop's door swung open and the enticing aroma of melted mozzarella wafted out. He forced a smile onto his face and went for a friendly chat with one of his teammates, still reeling from the lingering possibility that he just wouldn't fit in well enough to crack the lineup.

"Whaddaya think about getting drafted into Division III?" Marcus tossed down, laughing off any anxiety or disappointment.

Marcus's teammate shook his head good-humoredly and clapped him on the back. But Jena knew that even when they joked around with their teammates like brothers, everyone – especially the coaches – saw something else there too: performance. And right now, despite this pizza-fueled lightheartedness, Marcus felt a lingering sense he could easily get left out of tomorrow's lineup.

Tryouts were tomorrow – she could almost taste the adrenaline thrumming through her veins already.

"Hey kiddo, need a sandwich before dinner?" Alex's father called out over his shoulder, a hint of curiosity creeping into his tone.

As she shook off an uncharacteristic shiver and wrapped herself in a damp sweatshirt, she let the conversation lull for a moment. It must be something in the air that still kept them from really talking about what tomorrow meant – though every time someone walked by saying "you'll make it," she felt those same old flutters in her chest.

Her father handed her down a turkey sandwich and Alex gave him an absent-minded smile, eating on autopilot while listening to him say something completely unimportant, like whether they should get takeout or order pizza. Tomorrow, all of this – this whole life, his concern – would hang by an invisible thread that was starting to fray. She could almost hear the rustle of threads coming undone as their faces met in the garage's faint evening light.

The sun began setting when Alex turned her mind back to tomorrow at precisely what time she needed to be there – 7 AM sharp, no sleep-in – and suddenly they were walking out together into a crisp dusk that should've been bracing but now felt so full of weight.
